paras: The lynching of John Hollins took place near Drew, Mississippi, on the night of January 9, 1903, when a mob of masked men took Hollins, a Black man, off a train two miles south of the town and shot him to death. He had been charged with attempting a criminal assault upon a white girl. An Associated Press dispatch carried the killing to newspapers across the country, and Black weeklies later counted it in their records of the year's lynchings.

The only charge reported against Hollins was that he had attempted "a criminal assault upon a white girl." The coverage names neither the girl nor anyone who brought the charge, and it does not say whether Hollins had been arrested before the mob seized him.

According to the dispatch, datelined Drew on January 10, Hollins was taken off a train two miles south of the town "last night." The men who seized him wore masks and shot him to death, and the dispatch gave neither their number nor any names.
No report of an inquest, arrests or grand jury action appears in the coverage.

White newspapers printed the Associated Press dispatch on January 11 from Louisville and Richmond to Salt Lake City and San Francisco. Headlines named it plainly as mob killing or lynching, among them "Negro Lynched in Mississippi" in the Richmond Dispatch, "Mob in Masks Lynch a Negro" in the Raleigh News and Observer, and "MOB KILLS NEGRO" in the Wheeling Sunday Register. None of these papers added comment, and each repeated the charge as the dispatch gave it.

Over the following week, weekly news digests in Ohio, Wyoming, Idaho and Utah reduced the story to a single sentence among unrelated items. A different digest, printed in Mississippi weeklies at Lexington and Scranton, called him "John Hallings" and said the mob had "hanged" him.

Among Black papers, the Iowa Bystander ran a garbled copy of the wire brief on January 16 without comment. The next day the Indianapolis Freeman took up the case in an editorial without naming Hollins, describing a "colored man in Mississippi" pulled from a train on an assault charge, "which ended as usual; the colored man was shot." The Freeman held that the truth of the charge was "not the thing" and read the shooting as an expression of white "sentiment" on the "social question," which a Black man defied "at a very great risk." The same editorial praised Governor Longino's proclamation against whitecapping and urged Black readers to support it.

Later in 1903, the Wichita Searchlight and the Sedalia Times reprinted a record of lynchings that opened January with Hollins, killed by "lawless men" on a charge of attempted assault. The Seattle Republican printed a similar list under the heading "Mobocracy's Bloody Reign," and the Chicago Broad Ax included him in its chronology of the year's lynchings in January 1904.

The reports differ on how Hollins was killed: the dispatch from Drew said he was shot to death, while the Lexington Progress-Advertiser digest said he was hanged. The dispatch is the earlier report and carried a Drew dateline, whereas the hanging version appeared without a dateline in a condensed summary that also misspelled his name. The Black lynching records dated the killing January 10, the date of the dispatch, and the Iowa Bystander's copy carried a January 12 dateline, although the dispatch itself placed the seizure on the night before January 10.

reader.title: Lynching of John Hollins
bases: A mob of masked men took Hollins off a train and shot him to death on a charge of attempted assault on a white girl, and the Associated Press headline called it a lynching (A1, A4).

Hollins was shot to death by 'a mob of masked men' with no officer or legal process mentioned, after being charged with attempting a criminal assault on a white girl (A1, A3); headlines called it a lynching and Black papers counted it in their 1903 lynching records (A4, A20, A23).

Every contemporary report goes back to one Associated Press dispatch from Drew dated January 10 (A1, A4) or to digest rewrites of it (A9, A12); the Black lynching lists are later compilations (A20, A22). No independent local account was found.

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch from Drew
accounts.gist: Hollins, 'a negro', was taken off a train two miles south of Drew the night before by a mob of masked men and shot to death; he was charged with attempting a criminal assault on a white girl.

accounts.label: Ready-print news digest
accounts.gist: 'John Hallings, a negro' was taken off a train near Drew by a mob and hanged; he was accused of criminal assault.

accounts.label: Black lynching records
accounts.gist: Lists of 1903 lynchings enter John Hollins under January 10 at Drew, Miss., with the cause given as attempted (criminal) assault.

framing.detail: The AP dispatch ran unchanged under headlines such as 'Negro Lynched in Mississippi', 'Mob in Masks Lynch a Negro' and 'MOB KILLS NEGRO', stating the charge without comment.
Weekly news digests condensed it to a single line among unrelated items; one digest version said he was 'hanged'.
The Iowa Bystander ran a garbled copy of the wire brief without comment.

The Indianapolis Freeman called the outcome 'usual', said the truth of the charge was 'not the thing', and treated the shooting as a sign of white 'sentiment' that Black people should not defy, while praising Gov. Longino's stand against whitecapping.
Later lists counted Hollins among men killed by 'lawless men' or under the heading 'Mobocracy's Bloody Reign'.

conflicts.note: The shooting comes from the AP dispatch datelined Drew, the earliest report; 'hanged' appears only in an undated digest rewrite that also misspells the name, so the dispatch is the better evidence.

versions.value: night of January 9 ('last night' in a January 10 dispatch)

conflicts.note: The lists use the dispatch date; the Bystander's January 12 dateline appears to be a reprint error, since the dispatch ran on January 11.
Spelling variants in rewrites and lists.

record_check.dossier: The papers say only that he was taken off a train by a masked mob; none says he was under arrest or in an officer's custody.
No Hollins report names the county; a separate June 1903 Mississippi item places Drew in Sunflower County.

record_check.record: Date not given in the article.
record_check.dossier: The dispatch is dated January 10 and says 'last night', i.e. January 9.
Supported (taken off a train, shot to death); one digest says hanged instead of shot.
At least 6 Black-press items (Bystander, Freeman, three 1903 lynching lists, Broad Ax chronology) and more than a dozen white papers carried it.
